root_topic: The World of Metals and Non-metals

details: Malleability allows materials to be hammered into thin sheets (gold, silver, aluminium). Ductility allows drawing into thin wires (copper, iron). Metallic lustre gives fresh surfaces shiny reflection. Sonority produces ringing sound on striking.
evidence_or_examples: Sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a butter knife. Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

branches.theme: Section 4.2 Chemical Reactions with Oxygen and Water

sub_branches.concept: 4.2 Chemical Reactions with Oxygen and Water
details: Magnesium ribbon burns in oxygen with blinding white light to yield Magnesium Oxide (MgO), which dissolves in water forming Mg(OH)2 (turns red litmus blue = Basic). Sulfur burns forming Sulfur Dioxide (SO2), forming sulfurous acid in water (turns blue litmus red = Acidic). Iron rusts in moist air forming brown hydrated iron oxide.
evidence_or_examples: Everything in the universe is constructed from 118 chemical elements cataloged in the periodic table.

sub_branches.concept: To test materials for malleability by hammering.
details: Place each sample on an anvil surface.
Strike each sample firmly 3-4 times with a hammer.
Observe whether sample flattens into a sheet or breaks into pieces.
Observation: Iron nail and copper wire flatten into thin sheets without breaking. Coal and sulfur lump shatter into fine powder.
evidence_or_examples: Metals possess malleability (flatten under impact), while solid non-metals are brittle.

details: Malleability: The property of a material allowing it to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets.
Ductility: The property of a material enabling it to be drawn into thin wires.
evidence_or_examples: Aluminium foil for food packaging; gold foil.
Copper and copper alloy wires in electrical grids.
